title: A great idea that everyone hates
gist: Yglesias's free preview (the rest is paywalled) argues that the simplest available fix for high electricity bills is passing the wholesale spot price through to households, since residential customers currently pay an annualized average that is significantly higher on average than real-time cost. He concedes the idea is politically toxic, but argues the gains grow as electric appliances, EVs and cheap batteries spread, and that the profusion of complicated 'new' pricing schemes is an evasion of the straightforward option.

themes.theme: Spot-price pass-through as the unspoken fix

insights.claim: Charging household electricity users the wholesale spot price would meaningfully lower short-term prices without killing incentives for new generation investment.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Real-time retail pricing is the cheapest lever on power bills and would reprice demand-response, smart-thermostat and home-battery businesses if it ever advanced politically.
insights.quote: The simplest way to bring down utility bills is to charge what the electricity actually costs.

insights.claim: Households currently pay a kind of annualized average rather than fluctuating wholesale prices, which is far more convenient but involves significantly higher prices on average.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: The convenience premium embedded in flat residential tariffs is a hidden cost line — utilities that keep flat rates are effectively selling price insurance customers may not want.
insights.quote: Residential consumers, however, don’t pay these prices; what households pay instead is a kind of annualized average.
insights.locator: Residential consumers, however, don’t pay these prices

insights.claim: Nobody discusses spot-price pass-through because it is universally understood to be politically toxic, which impoverishes the debate and produces a stream of complicated 'new' schemes that are really just spot pricing with extra bells and whistles.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Treat elaborate new retail-rate proposals as reinvented dynamic pricing; the political constraint, not the technical design, is what determines whether any of them ship.
insights.quote: nobody in their right mind even talks about this idea because it’s universally understood to be politically toxic and something everyone would hate
insights.locator: The bad news is that nobody in their right mind

insights.claim: On July 15, 2026 in New England, unusually smoky conditions pushed solar power production below the seasonal average, illustrating how weather shocks swing wholesale power supply.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Smoke — not just clouds — is a solar generation risk factor that grids with high solar penetration must increasingly hedge.
insights.quote: On July 15 in New England, for example, it was unusually smoky, thereby putting solar power production below the seasonal average.
insights.locator: Electricity grids must constantly balance supply and demand

insights.claim: On July 17, 2026, grid congestion produced a period of negative electricity prices in a specific part of Maine, while retail customers in that area saw no benefit.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Localized negative pricing marks where transmission constraints — not generation shortfalls — bind; those nodes are the highest-value sites for storage and flexible load.
insights.quote: on July 17, there was a weird occurrence where grid congestion led to a period of negative prices in the specific part of Maine where I am
insights.locator: Then on July 17, there was a weird occurrence

insights.claim: The potential gains from spot pricing grow as more households adopt electric appliances and cars and as batteries become cheaper and more widely available, because these loads can be shifted in time.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Cheap storage plus flexible electrified load makes dynamic-pricing value compound over time — the case for the policy strengthens each year even as its politics stay unchanged.
insights.quote: as more people get electric appliances and cars and as batteries become cheaper and more widely available, the potential gains of forcing everyone to pay the spot price grow
insights.locator: And as more people get electric appliances

insights.claim: The practical objection to real-time retail pricing is user experience — needing an app that sends emergency notifications when electricity spikes to quintuple its normal price so consumers can change the thermostat before going broke.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Automation that removes the consumer from the loop is the precondition for dynamic pricing to become politically viable — the opportunity sits with smart-device and home-energy-management vendors.
insights.quote: That’s a lot more convenient than having an app that gives you an emergency notification that electricity has spiked to quintuple its normal price and you’d better change the thermostat before you go broke.
